analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans to cover three primary care and three mental health visits with no copays.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from its introduction in September 2022 until Congress ended in January 2023, with only two senators supporting it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal insurance law to require group health plans and individual health insurance plans to pay the full cost of three primary care visits and three behavioral health visits each year — no copays, deductibles, or other out-of-pocket charges. It also made sure plans couldn't count these visits against stricter limits or pay providers less for them, and it allowed these visits to be covered even under high-deductible health plans. The rules would have taken effect two years after enactment. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with private health insurance who needs to see a doctor or a mental health provider but puts it off because of copays or deductibles. The bill would have made the first three primary care visits and first three behavioral health visits each year free at the point of care, and would have guaranteed those visits counted the same as any other visit and paid providers the same rates. People in high-deductible plans — where patients pay thousands out of pocket before insurance kicks in — would have benefited particularly, since the bill allowed these visits to be covered before the deductible was met.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured people facing copays for care

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and individual health insurance to cover three primary care visits and three behavioral health visits per plan year with no cost sharing of any kind, on top of the preventive services already required under federal law.

Bars plans from applying separate treatment limits to those six visits and requires plans to reimburse them at the same rates as any other primary or behavioral health visit, so the free visits couldn't be quietly devalued.

Defines qualified behavioral providers broadly — including social workers, counselors, psychologists, psychiatric nurses, and marriage and family therapists — so the free mental health visits could be used with the providers patients actually see.
Changes high-deductible health plan rules so these visits could be covered before the deductible was met, letting people in those plans use them without paying thousands out of pocket first.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group health plans would bear the cost of covering the six visits without collecting copays or deductible payments, and that cost could show up partly in premiums or reduced benefits elsewhere.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The mandate is narrow: three visits per year each for primary and behavioral care is a small fraction of typical care needs, and people with serious conditions would still face cost sharing after those visits run out.
The cost of the free visits falls on insurers and employer plans, which could pass it through as somewhat higher premiums for everyone with private coverage.
The changes would not have taken effect until two years after enactment, delaying any benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A real but modest benefit: six free visits a year meaningfully lowers the barrier for people who skip checkups or therapy over copays, especially those in high-deductible plans, and the bill's anti-workaround rules (same limits, same reimbursement) made the mandate hard to evade. The main honest cost is that insurers and employers absorb those visits and may fold part of it into premiums, and three visits is a small floor rather than a fix for broader cost-sharing problems.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or markup, and died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Angus King introduced the bill on September 21, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
One Senate Democrat cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors signed on.
The Finance Committee took no action — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote appear in the bill's action history after the referral.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers offering group plans are better off, since they avoid a mandate to cover six visits a year without cost sharing; the roughly 47 million insured people who might have used the free visits are not.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support was Sen. King and one Democratic cosponsor, with no Republican cosponsors, so any partisan shape has to be inferred from that.

industries.note: They would have had to cover six visits a year with no copays or deductible payments, absorbing that cost in claims rather than collecting it from patients. Insured patients' gain — free access to primary and mental health care — is exactly the cost insurers would have borne.

ERISA-covered group plans would face the same mandate, and the bill also amended the tax code provisions governing high-deductible employer plans. Employers funding those plans would pick up part of the added cost.

industries.industry: Primary care and behavioral health providers
industries.note: The first three primary and three behavioral visits would be fully reimbursed at standard plan rates, removing a barrier that keeps patients from booking appointments. Providers get paid while patients pay nothing.
